items.author: Gwyneth Paltrow

items.title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
items.abstract: This paper introduces "bottling," the ability of LLM agents to autonomously create cost-effective, task-specific solutions for large workloads. The core method involves agents deciding how to tackle an entire unlabelled dataset within fixed resource budgets, potentially by training smaller models or writing programs. The key contribution is demonstrating that strong general LLM performance doesn't guarantee good "bottling" capabilities, with many agents failing to match their zero-shot performance when tasked with creating scalable artifacts.

items.title: Principled Under Pressure: Post-Training Decides Whether LLMs Act on Their Own Moral Judgment
items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel method to evaluate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) act on their own moral judgments when faced with pressure. By posing scenarios twice – once as an agent's decision and once as a third-person judgment – the researchers can identify when models violate their own stated values. The key contribution is demonstrating that post-training methods significantly influence an LLM's ability to resist pressure and adhere to its internal moral compass.

items.title: ScienceClaw: Benchmarking Continual Self-Evolution of AI-for-Science Agents Across the Natural and Social Sciences
items.abstract: This paper introduces ScienceClaw, a framework for benchmarking the continual self-evolution of AI-for-science agents. Its core method is fixed-parameter program self-evolution, which integrates task solving, scientific verification, and program updates. ScienceClaw's contribution lies in its comprehensive evaluation across 23 disciplines, measuring scientific correctness, evolutionary gain, and retention, addressing the gap in current evaluations that don't track persistent program improvements in sequential tasks across natural and social sciences.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. Task formulation of verifiable program-level self-evolution for AI-for-Science agents. Scientific tasks and domain constraints form sequential task streams. ScienceClaw uses a fixed foundation model with editable Skills and typed Operators to construct executable workflows, and evaluates repairs by source replay, independent validation, transfer, retention, and cost.

items.title: Semantic Behavioral Watermarking: Paraphrase-Robust and Forgery-Resistant Provenance for LLM Agents
items.abstract: This paper introduces Semantic Behavioral Watermarking (SBW), a novel method for embedding provenance in LLM agents' high-level action choices, independent of output tokens. SBW achieves paraphrase robustness by watermarking semantic action clusters and is forgery-resistant through keyed collision-resistant binning, addressing limitations of prior agent watermarking techniques. Its core contribution is providing a more secure and adaptable provenance mechanism for LLM agents.

items.title: SquidAgent: Parallelize Wisely, Coordinate Efficiently
items.abstract: This paper introduces SquidAgent, a method for parallelizing LLM-based agents to reduce latency in multi-step tasks. It addresses the inefficiency of existing parallel systems by identifying and mitigating "re-exploration" and "alignment" costs. SquidAgent proposes a principled criterion to determine when parallelization is beneficial, aiming for near-linear speedups by avoiding redundant work and reconciling inconsistencies.

items.title: Toward Alignment Scaling Laws: A Framework and First Preregistered Measurements
items.abstract: This paper proposes a framework to study how model alignment scales with capability, treating alignment as a family of measurable scaling relations rather than a single property. The core method models the "alignment burden" for different risk categories as a power law of model capability, allowing researchers to predict whether alignment becomes easier or harder as models grow. The key contribution is this quantitative approach to understanding alignment scaling, providing preregistered measurements and theoretical insights into the long-term implications of different scaling exponents.

items.title: WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
items.abstract: WorldSolver introduces a benchmark of 168 physics simulation tasks from computer graphics to evaluate LLM agents' ability to generate physics solvers. The core method involves LLM agents completing code scaffolds by implementing the underlying physical dynamics for given scenarios. This work contributes by exploring and evaluating LLMs' potential for simulating complex physical phenomena, a crucial step for applications in embodied AI and other fields.
items.figure_caption: Example of a WorldSolver task. Given a task description and a fixed code scaffold, an agent constructs a physics solver leveraging physical understanding, mathematical modeling, and software engineering. The solver advances the system state over time, producing a state trajectory that is rendered into a simulation video. Scene geometry, physical inputs, and rendering settings remain fixed across agents.

items.title: Towards In-Parameter Memory Augmentation for Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper surveys methods for augmenting Large Language Models (LLMs) with "in-parameter memory." The core method involves integrating reusable memory information directly into model parameters or parameter-like objects that are composed during inference. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of in-context learning by providing a more efficient and scalable way to incorporate post-pretraining knowledge.
items.figure_caption: A demonstration of the representative methods in the two-dimensional taxonomy.

items.title: Adaptive Power Sampling for LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), a method to improve LLM reasoning by adjusting the "sharpening" of the model's output distribution on a per-query basis. Unlike previous uniform approaches, APS leverages the relationship between answer agreement and the model's self-reward to dynamically determine the optimal sharpening level for each query. This adaptive strategy leads to consistent performance gains across various reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: AdvSim2Real : Training Web Agents Against Adaptive Prompt Injection in a Web World Model
items.abstract: This paper introduces AdvSim2Real, a method for training web agents to resist prompt injection attacks. It co-evolves the agent, a task curriculum, and an injection adversary within a simulated web environment. This approach allows the agent to become more capable and robust by continuously adapting to new attacks and tasks, unlike previous methods that relied on fixed injections or tasks.

items.title: How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation
items.abstract: This paper introduces Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD) to improve coding agents' self-correction learning. EESD adaptively weights corrections based on execution support and evidence strength, unlike fixed weighting methods. This approach significantly reduces future prediction errors by better leveraging self-correction feedback.
items.figure_caption: Direction and strength in a coding agent’s self-correction. (a) Fixing an off-by-one range error changes four public executions from fail to pass. (b) Aggregating execution relevance by transition gives r = ( 1 , 0 , 0 , 0 ) r=(1,0,0,0) : all support favors Fix . (c) The same transitions under uniform and concentrated relevance give E ⁡ ( p ) = 4.000 E(p)=4.000 and 1.062 1.062 ; at fixed prior and utility settings, they yield different supervised weights. The p p bars index executions, whereas the r r bars index transition categories. The relevance vectors define an analytical example at fixed transition support.

items.title: Latent space bias directions in LLMs capture confidence, not fairness
items.abstract: This paper investigates the debiasing direction used in activation steering for LLMs. It finds that this direction primarily captures model confidence, steering towards lower-probability tokens, rather than representing actual bias. Consequently, while it reduces measured bias, it does so by making the model less confident, potentially leading to abstention on tasks.
items.figure_caption: Figure 1. An illustration of the paper’s two central claims, for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Left : distribution of the linear classifier bias score P ⁡ ( biased ) P(\( \mathrm{biased} \)) , trained on ambiguous BBQ contexts, evaluated on BBQ disambiguated contexts and labelled as biased (pink) or anti-biased (teal) answer type. The linear classifier poorly separates the biased and anti-biased prompts, achieving an AUROC of only 0.57. Centre : Same as the left panel but labelled by whether the scored answer is the model’s highest- (purple) or lowest- (green) probability choice. The classifier achieves a higher separability on confidence than on bias, with an AUROC of 0.94. Right : mean probability assigned to biased (pink), anti-biased (teal) and neutral/abstain (grey) answers on BBQ (ambig.) as a function of activation-steering strength \( \alpha \) along the debiasing direction. Steering increases the rate of abstention rather than correcting the underlying biased/anti-biased preference, consistent with the direction being dominated by confidence rather than bias. Bias-probe scores separate by confidence far better than by bias class; steering increases abstention. Three-panel figure. Left: histograms of the probe's bias score for biased versus anti-biased answers on BBQ disambiguated questions – the two distributions overlap almost completely (AUROC 0.57). Middle: the same scores split instead by whether the answer was the model's highest- or lowest-probability choice – the distributions separate almost completely (AUROC 0.94). Right: mean answer probability against steering strength $\( \alpha \)$ from $-1$ to $2$ for biased, anti-biased, and neutral (abstain) answers – the biased and anti-biased curves decline together from about 0.5 to 0.2, while the neutral curve rises from near 0 to about 0.65 and comes to dominate.

items.title: MINDSET: Energy-based Schema Evolution for Long Conversational Agent Memory
items.abstract: MINDSET addresses the challenge of long-term memory for conversational agents by organizing past interactions into versioned schemas. It achieves this through energy-based state transitions, where new conversational episodes are integrated by minimizing distortion, contradiction, and inconsistency. This approach allows agents to adapt to changing context while efficiently retrieving relevant information without constant LLM re-computation.
items.figure_caption: MINDSET stores immutable episodes, chooses minimum-energy transitions over versioned schemas, expands retrieved schemas back to provenance, and sends a bounded raw-evidence packet to the answer model.

items.title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
items.abstract: nanoMuse provides an open-source personal agent designed to operate across all of a user's devices. Its core method involves a distributed architecture where agents on each device communicate through a shared relay, enabling persistent, multi-device conversations and actions. The key contribution is offering a transparent, user-controlled alternative to proprietary cloud-based agents, emphasizing local control and data privacy.
items.figure_caption: One agent on every device, one conversation between them. Android and the desktop carry the whole agent and have hands on their own screens; the iPhone has everything but the hands, since iOS lets no app operate another; the web app shows the same conversation from a runtime on a computer of the person’s own. The devices meet over the relay, open source and optional; the screens are drawings, not screenshots.

items.title: One for All, All for One: Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering via Stochastic Optimal Control
items.abstract: This paper introduces Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering (CMDS), a method that reuses pre-trained diffusion models as independent component generators. CMDS learns a control mechanism to coordinate these frozen models, treating the problem as stochastic optimal control. This approach balances a global reward for the combined output with adherence to individual model dynamics, enabling efficient generation of structured outputs with desired properties.
items.figure_caption: Overview of CMDS . Frozen component diffusion models are sampled concurrently, while a joint control conditions on the multi-agent state and applies component-wise controls throughout the reverse process, yielding a coordinated assembled output.

items.title: Secure Speculative Decoding for Large Language Models
items.abstract: This paper introduces the first systematic study of security vulnerabilities in speculative decoding for LLMs. It reveals a significant trade-off where efficiency gains from speculative decoding disproportionately increase the risk of jailbreak and prompt injection attacks. The authors then propose SecureSD to address these security concerns.

items.title: Sherpa: Teaching LLMs to Teach Adaptively
items.abstract: Sherpa is a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to teach by directly optimizing student learning outcomes. It addresses the limitation of existing methods by simulating diverse student archetypes with unique learning preferences and adapting the teacher's instruction accordingly. This adaptive approach significantly improves student performance across different learner types.
items.figure_caption: Overview of our framework. The teacher interacts with student archetypes through preparation, tutoring, and testing, and receives a reward for tutoring based on the student’s improvement. The student archetype is implemented by a backbone model with a gating mechanism.

items.title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
items.abstract: VeriFine addresses the bottleneck of fixed judges in self-improving embodied reasoning agents. Its core method is a co-evolutionary framework where the policy, training curriculum, and judge adapt together. This allows the agent to scale verification, discover new failure patterns, and ultimately achieve more robust self-improvement by incorporating human feedback to refine the judge.

items.title: Wiki-Talkie: Multilingual Benchmarking of Persona-Based Agents on Real-World Discussions
items.abstract: This paper introduces Wiki-Talkie, a multilingual dataset of real-world Wikipedia talk page conversations paired with realistic user personas. Its core method involves using this dataset to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on their ability to generate human-like dialogue based on these grounded personas. The main contribution is providing a robust, multilingual benchmark for assessing the behavioral fidelity of persona-based LLM agents in simulating real-world social interactions.
items.figure_caption: Example from Wiki-Talkie with its three core components: article , thread , and persona .

items.title: Agentic AutoRAG: RAG Pipeline Optimization through Reasoning-Driven Agents
items.abstract: Agentic AutoRAG optimizes RAG pipelines by using LLM agents to reason about hyperparameter choices. Its core method involves a "Diagnoser" agent that attributes failures to either retrieval or generation stages, and a "Proposer" agent that suggests new configurations based on this diagnosis and a knowledge base of model performance and cost. This approach moves beyond simple aggregate scores to a more intelligent, failure-aware optimization process.

items.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

items.description: The design language that makes your AI harness better at design.

items.summary: This repository enables persistent context for AI agents by capturing, compressing, and re-injecting session data, enhancing future interactions across various AI models.

items.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.
items.summary: This repository provides a skill for coding agents to prevent them from burying answers, offering ADHD-friendly output that keeps crucial information accessible.

items.description: Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries.
items.summary: This repository provides agents for reverse engineering, enabling the analysis of application behavior and native binaries.

items.description: DeepGEMM: clean and efficient BLAS kernel library on GPU
items.summary: DeepGEMM is a clean and efficient BLAS kernel library for GPUs, designed to accelerate linear algebra operations.

arxiv.title: Agentic AutoRAG: RAG Pipeline Optimization through Reasoning-Driven Agents
arxiv.abstract: Agentic AutoRAG optimizes RAG pipelines by using LLM agents to reason about hyperparameter choices. Its core method involves a "Diagnoser" agent that attributes failures to either retrieval or generation stages, and a "Proposer" agent that suggests new configurations based on this diagnosis and a knowledge base of model performance and cost. This approach moves beyond simple aggregate scores to a more intelligent, failure-aware optimization process.

papers.title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
papers.abstract: This paper introduces "bottling," the ability of LLM agents to autonomously create cost-effective, task-specific solutions for large workloads. The core method involves agents deciding how to tackle an entire unlabelled dataset within fixed resource budgets, potentially by training smaller models or writing programs. The key contribution is demonstrating that strong general LLM performance doesn't guarantee good "bottling" capabilities, with many agents failing to match their zero-shot performance when tasked with creating scalable artifacts.

papers.title: Principled Under Pressure: Post-Training Decides Whether LLMs Act on Their Own Moral Judgment
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel method to evaluate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) act on their own moral judgments when faced with pressure. By posing scenarios twice – once as an agent's decision and once as a third-person judgment – the researchers can identify when models violate their own stated values. The key contribution is demonstrating that post-training methods significantly influence an LLM's ability to resist pressure and adhere to its internal moral compass.

papers.title: ScienceClaw: Benchmarking Continual Self-Evolution of AI-for-Science Agents Across the Natural and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: This paper introduces ScienceClaw, a framework for benchmarking the continual self-evolution of AI-for-science agents. Its core method is fixed-parameter program self-evolution, which integrates task solving, scientific verification, and program updates. ScienceClaw's contribution lies in its comprehensive evaluation across 23 disciplines, measuring scientific correctness, evolutionary gain, and retention, addressing the gap in current evaluations that don't track persistent program improvements in sequential tasks across natural and social sciences.
papers.figure_caption: Figure 1. Task formulation of verifiable program-level self-evolution for AI-for-Science agents. Scientific tasks and domain constraints form sequential task streams. ScienceClaw uses a fixed foundation model with editable Skills and typed Operators to construct executable workflows, and evaluates repairs by source replay, independent validation, transfer, retention, and cost.

papers.title: Semantic Behavioral Watermarking: Paraphrase-Robust and Forgery-Resistant Provenance for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Semantic Behavioral Watermarking (SBW), a novel method for embedding provenance in LLM agents' high-level action choices, independent of output tokens. SBW achieves paraphrase robustness by watermarking semantic action clusters and is forgery-resistant through keyed collision-resistant binning, addressing limitations of prior agent watermarking techniques. Its core contribution is providing a more secure and adaptable provenance mechanism for LLM agents.

papers.title: SquidAgent: Parallelize Wisely, Coordinate Efficiently
papers.abstract: This paper introduces SquidAgent, a method for parallelizing LLM-based agents to reduce latency in multi-step tasks. It addresses the inefficiency of existing parallel systems by identifying and mitigating "re-exploration" and "alignment" costs. SquidAgent proposes a principled criterion to determine when parallelization is beneficial, aiming for near-linear speedups by avoiding redundant work and reconciling inconsistencies.

papers.title: Toward Alignment Scaling Laws: A Framework and First Preregistered Measurements
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a framework to study how model alignment scales with capability, treating alignment as a family of measurable scaling relations rather than a single property. The core method models the "alignment burden" for different risk categories as a power law of model capability, allowing researchers to predict whether alignment becomes easier or harder as models grow. The key contribution is this quantitative approach to understanding alignment scaling, providing preregistered measurements and theoretical insights into the long-term implications of different scaling exponents.

papers.title: WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
papers.abstract: WorldSolver introduces a benchmark of 168 physics simulation tasks from computer graphics to evaluate LLM agents' ability to generate physics solvers. The core method involves LLM agents completing code scaffolds by implementing the underlying physical dynamics for given scenarios. This work contributes by exploring and evaluating LLMs' potential for simulating complex physical phenomena, a crucial step for applications in embodied AI and other fields.
papers.figure_caption: Example of a WorldSolver task. Given a task description and a fixed code scaffold, an agent constructs a physics solver leveraging physical understanding, mathematical modeling, and software engineering. The solver advances the system state over time, producing a state trajectory that is rendered into a simulation video. Scene geometry, physical inputs, and rendering settings remain fixed across agents.

papers.title: Towards In-Parameter Memory Augmentation for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper surveys methods for augmenting Large Language Models (LLMs) with "in-parameter memory." The core method involves integrating reusable memory information directly into model parameters or parameter-like objects that are composed during inference. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of in-context learning by providing a more efficient and scalable way to incorporate post-pretraining knowledge.
papers.figure_caption: A demonstration of the representative methods in the two-dimensional taxonomy.

papers.title: Adaptive Power Sampling for LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Power Sampling (APS), a method to improve LLM reasoning by adjusting the "sharpening" of the model's output distribution on a per-query basis. Unlike previous uniform approaches, APS leverages the relationship between answer agreement and the model's self-reward to dynamically determine the optimal sharpening level for each query. This adaptive strategy leads to consistent performance gains across various reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: AdvSim2Real : Training Web Agents Against Adaptive Prompt Injection in a Web World Model
papers.abstract: This paper introduces AdvSim2Real, a method for training web agents to resist prompt injection attacks. It co-evolves the agent, a task curriculum, and an injection adversary within a simulated web environment. This approach allows the agent to become more capable and robust by continuously adapting to new attacks and tasks, unlike previous methods that relied on fixed injections or tasks.

papers.title: How Much Evidence Should a Coding Agent's Self-Correction Carry? Adaptive Dirichlet Evidence for Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Effective-Evidence Self-Distillation (EESD) to improve coding agents' self-correction learning. EESD adaptively weights corrections based on execution support and evidence strength, unlike fixed weighting methods. This approach significantly reduces future prediction errors by better leveraging self-correction feedback.
papers.figure_caption: Direction and strength in a coding agent’s self-correction. (a) Fixing an off-by-one range error changes four public executions from fail to pass. (b) Aggregating execution relevance by transition gives r = ( 1 , 0 , 0 , 0 ) r=(1,0,0,0) : all support favors Fix . (c) The same transitions under uniform and concentrated relevance give E ⁡ ( p ) = 4.000 E(p)=4.000 and 1.062 1.062 ; at fixed prior and utility settings, they yield different supervised weights. The p p bars index executions, whereas the r r bars index transition categories. The relevance vectors define an analytical example at fixed transition support.

papers.title: Latent space bias directions in LLMs capture confidence, not fairness
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the debiasing direction used in activation steering for LLMs. It finds that this direction primarily captures model confidence, steering towards lower-probability tokens, rather than representing actual bias. Consequently, while it reduces measured bias, it does so by making the model less confident, potentially leading to abstention on tasks.
papers.figure_caption: Figure 1. An illustration of the paper’s two central claims, for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Left : distribution of the linear classifier bias score P ⁡ ( biased ) P(\( \mathrm{biased} \)) , trained on ambiguous BBQ contexts, evaluated on BBQ disambiguated contexts and labelled as biased (pink) or anti-biased (teal) answer type. The linear classifier poorly separates the biased and anti-biased prompts, achieving an AUROC of only 0.57. Centre : Same as the left panel but labelled by whether the scored answer is the model’s highest- (purple) or lowest- (green) probability choice. The classifier achieves a higher separability on confidence than on bias, with an AUROC of 0.94. Right : mean probability assigned to biased (pink), anti-biased (teal) and neutral/abstain (grey) answers on BBQ (ambig.) as a function of activation-steering strength \( \alpha \) along the debiasing direction. Steering increases the rate of abstention rather than correcting the underlying biased/anti-biased preference, consistent with the direction being dominated by confidence rather than bias. Bias-probe scores separate by confidence far better than by bias class; steering increases abstention. Three-panel figure. Left: histograms of the probe's bias score for biased versus anti-biased answers on BBQ disambiguated questions – the two distributions overlap almost completely (AUROC 0.57). Middle: the same scores split instead by whether the answer was the model's highest- or lowest-probability choice – the distributions separate almost completely (AUROC 0.94). Right: mean answer probability against steering strength $\( \alpha \)$ from $-1$ to $2$ for biased, anti-biased, and neutral (abstain) answers – the biased and anti-biased curves decline together from about 0.5 to 0.2, while the neutral curve rises from near 0 to about 0.65 and comes to dominate.

papers.title: MINDSET: Energy-based Schema Evolution for Long Conversational Agent Memory
papers.abstract: MINDSET addresses the challenge of long-term memory for conversational agents by organizing past interactions into versioned schemas. It achieves this through energy-based state transitions, where new conversational episodes are integrated by minimizing distortion, contradiction, and inconsistency. This approach allows agents to adapt to changing context while efficiently retrieving relevant information without constant LLM re-computation.
papers.figure_caption: MINDSET stores immutable episodes, chooses minimum-energy transitions over versioned schemas, expands retrieved schemas back to provenance, and sends a bounded raw-evidence packet to the answer model.

papers.title: nanoMuse: An Open-Source Personal Agent for Every Device You Own
papers.abstract: nanoMuse provides an open-source personal agent designed to operate across all of a user's devices. Its core method involves a distributed architecture where agents on each device communicate through a shared relay, enabling persistent, multi-device conversations and actions. The key contribution is offering a transparent, user-controlled alternative to proprietary cloud-based agents, emphasizing local control and data privacy.
papers.figure_caption: One agent on every device, one conversation between them. Android and the desktop carry the whole agent and have hands on their own screens; the iPhone has everything but the hands, since iOS lets no app operate another; the web app shows the same conversation from a runtime on a computer of the person’s own. The devices meet over the relay, open source and optional; the screens are drawings, not screenshots.

papers.title: One for All, All for One: Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering via Stochastic Optimal Control
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering (CMDS), a method that reuses pre-trained diffusion models as independent component generators. CMDS learns a control mechanism to coordinate these frozen models, treating the problem as stochastic optimal control. This approach balances a global reward for the combined output with adherence to individual model dynamics, enabling efficient generation of structured outputs with desired properties.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of CMDS . Frozen component diffusion models are sampled concurrently, while a joint control conditions on the multi-agent state and applies component-wise controls throughout the reverse process, yielding a coordinated assembled output.

papers.title: Secure Speculative Decoding for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the first systematic study of security vulnerabilities in speculative decoding for LLMs. It reveals a significant trade-off where efficiency gains from speculative decoding disproportionately increase the risk of jailbreak and prompt injection attacks. The authors then propose SecureSD to address these security concerns.

papers.title: Sherpa: Teaching LLMs to Teach Adaptively
papers.abstract: Sherpa is a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to teach by directly optimizing student learning outcomes. It addresses the limitation of existing methods by simulating diverse student archetypes with unique learning preferences and adapting the teacher's instruction accordingly. This adaptive approach significantly improves student performance across different learner types.
papers.figure_caption: Overview of our framework. The teacher interacts with student archetypes through preparation, tutoring, and testing, and receives a reward for tutoring based on the student’s improvement. The student archetype is implemented by a backbone model with a gating mechanism.

papers.title: VeriFine: Scaling Verification for Self-Improvement in Embodied Reasoning
papers.abstract: VeriFine addresses the bottleneck of fixed judges in self-improving embodied reasoning agents. Its core method is a co-evolutionary framework where the policy, training curriculum, and judge adapt together. This allows the agent to scale verification, discover new failure patterns, and ultimately achieve more robust self-improvement by incorporating human feedback to refine the judge.

papers.title: Wiki-Talkie: Multilingual Benchmarking of Persona-Based Agents on Real-World Discussions
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Wiki-Talkie, a multilingual dataset of real-world Wikipedia talk page conversations paired with realistic user personas. Its core method involves using this dataset to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on their ability to generate human-like dialogue based on these grounded personas. The main contribution is providing a robust, multilingual benchmark for assessing the behavioral fidelity of persona-based LLM agents in simulating real-world social interactions.
papers.figure_caption: Example from Wiki-Talkie with its three core components: article , thread , and persona .
